entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (her car), plural countable (her keys), uncountable (her patience) — and gerunds (her leaving). Never another central determiner: ✗ the her car, ✗ a her friend. Never stands alone with no noun after it — that is the pronoun hers.
entries.ofRule: Takes no of-phrase of its own. When of appears before her, it belongs to a preceding quantifier: all of her friends, most of her time, neither of her options. The double genitive requires the pronoun: a friend of hers, never ✗ a friend of her.
entries.pattern: her [noun] · [predeterminer] her [noun] — all her cousins, half her paycheck · her [ordinal] [cardinal] [adjective] [noun] — her first two real jobs · her own [noun] · [quantifier] of her [noun]
entries.contrast: English has three hers. The determiner precedes a noun (her coat); the object pronoun follows a verb or preposition (I called her, with her); the possessive pronoun hers stands alone (the coat is hers). The spelling ✗ her's is never correct. Against his: the choice tracks the possessor's gender, not the noun's — Maria called her brother, David called his mother.
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to, produced by, or associated with a female person or animal already identified. 1. The ordinary possessive. 2. A dated and now largely poetic use for ships, countries, and machines (the ship and her crew). Modern American usage, including AP style, writes its here.
examples: Her apartment is two blocks from the office. (singular countable)
Maria left her keys, her badge, and her laptop on the desk. (plural countable)
I admire her patience with that class. (uncountable)
All her cousins flew in for the wedding. (predeterminer all, no of)
She started the company with her own savings.
I appreciated her driving me to the airport. (gerund)
Isn't that her car in the driveway? (question — the determiner does not change)
She hasn't returned her library books. (negative)
The ship and her crew reached port at dawn. (sense 2, dated — modern American writing uses its)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (his phone), plural countable (his parents), uncountable (his luggage) — and gerunds (his quitting). Never with another central determiner: ✗ the his phone.
entries.ofRule: No of-phrase of its own; of before his belongs to a preceding quantifier: both of his sisters, none of his excuses. The double genitive uses the identical form: a cousin of his.
entries.pattern: his [noun] · [predeterminer] his [noun] — all his friends, both his brothers · his [ordinal] [cardinal] [noun] — his first three albums · his own [noun] · a [noun] of his
entries.contrast: his is the one possessive whose determiner and pronoun forms are identical: his car (determiner, noun follows) versus the car is his (pronoun, nothing follows). Compare her/hers, your/yours, our/ours, their/theirs. Against generic their: older writing used his for a person of unknown gender (Every student must bring his book); modern American writing uses singular their or, in formal prose, his or her.
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to, produced by, or associated with a male person or animal already identified. 1. The ordinary possessive. 2. The generic masculine, covering a person of unspecified gender. Standard until the 1970s, now avoided in American editing — replace with singular their, with his or her, or by making the subject plural.
examples: His flight lands at six. (singular countable)
David forgot his wallet, his phone, and his charger. (plural countable)
The airline lost his luggage in Denver. (uncountable)
Both his brothers work downtown. (predeterminer both, no of)
He paid the deposit out of his own savings.
Every applicant should submit his résumé by Friday. (dated generic — today, their résumé)
Didn't he bring his laptop? (question)
He never answers his phone after six. (negative)

entries.ipa: /ɪts/ — no separate weak form. Alone among the personal possessives, its does not reduce: unstressed it stays /ɪts/, exactly like it's
entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (its handle), plural countable (its wheels), uncountable (its funding) — and gerunds (its failing). The possessor is a thing, a place, an organization, an abstraction, or an animal whose sex is unstated; not a named person. Never another central determiner: ✗ the its logo.
entries.ofRule: None of its own. Of before its belongs to a preceding quantifier: most of its revenue, half of its board. There is no double-genitive form — ✗ a page of its is impossible; say one of its pages.
entries.pattern: its [noun] · [predeterminer] its [noun] — all its employees, half its budget · its own [noun] · [quantifier] of its [noun]
entries.contrast: its versus it's is the most-corrected error in written English. Its is the possessive determiner and never takes an apostrophe (the dog wagged its tail). It's is the contraction of it is or it has (it's raining, it's been a week). The test: if you can expand the word to it is or it has, write it's; otherwise write its. The form ✗ its' does not exist in English in any sense. Note also that the possessive-pronoun slot is empty here: there is no ✗ the tail is its — rewrite as the tail is the dog's.
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as a part, property, product, or possession of a thing, an animal, an institution, or an idea already mentioned.
examples: The dog chased its tail for ten minutes. (singular countable)
The company changed its logo again.
Portland is famous for its bridges. (plural countable)
The startup ran through its funding in a year. (uncountable)
Every state sets its own speed limits. (every + singular countable, singular verb sets)
The bill passed on its third reading.
Doesn't the museum publish its attendance numbers? (question)
The city has never released its full report. (negative)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (my car), plural countable (my parents), uncountable (my luggage) — plus gerunds (my leaving) and vocative address terms (my friend, my dear). Never another central determiner: ✗ the my car, ✗ a my friend.
entries.ofRule: None of its own; of before my belongs to a preceding quantifier (all of my cousins, neither of my options, a couple of my coworkers). The double genitive requires the pronoun mine: a friend of mine, ✗ a friend of my.
entries.pattern: my [noun] · [predeterminer] my [noun] — all my cousins, half my paycheck, both my sisters · my [ordinal] [cardinal] [adjective] [noun] — my first two real jobs · my own [noun] · my [gerund] — my leaving early
entries.contrast: my precedes a noun, mine stands alone: my seat versus that seat is mine. Modern English does not use mine as a determiner except in the frozen archaisms mine eyes and mine host (see mine). Do not confuse the possessive with the object pronoun me: ✓ He gave me my ticket, ✗ He gave my me ticket.
variants: mine /maɪn/ (MYNE) — not a separate word but the archaic prevocalic shape of this same determiner, standing before a vowel sound exactly as an does: mine eyes, mine own, mine host, mine enemy. It is the thy ~ thine alternation one person over, and it is dead outside quotation. Keep prenominal mine apart from standalone mine, which is a pronoun, not a determiner: mine eyes (noun follows — determiner) versus that seat is mine (nothing follows — pronoun). See mine for the register, the h- extension, and the examples.
dialectal me — me dad, me mum (British, Irish, and Australian speech; not standard American)
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to, produced by, or associated with the speaker. 1. The ordinary possessive. 2. In direct address, marking closeness or (often) condescension: my friend, my dear, my good man. 3. Before a gerund, naming the doer of the action: They didn't appreciate my leaving early.
examples: My keys are in my other jacket. (plural countable, then singular countable)
All my cousins live in Ohio. (predeterminer all; all of my cousins is equally correct)
She was my first real boss.
I paid for it with my own money. (uncountable)
They didn't appreciate my leaving early. (gerund)
My friend, that is not how this works. (vocative)
Have you seen my charger anywhere? (question)
I can't find my passport. (negative)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (our house), plural countable (our kids), uncountable (our luggage) — and gerunds (our leaving). Never another central determiner: ✗ the our house.
entries.ofRule: None of its own; of before our belongs to a preceding quantifier: several of our clients, most of our time. The double genitive uses ours: a neighbor of ours.
entries.pattern: our [noun] · [predeterminer] our [noun] — all our neighbors, half our budget · our [ordinal] [cardinal] [noun] — our first two attempts · our own [noun] · [quantifier] of our [noun]
entries.contrast: our precedes a noun, ours stands alone: our table versus the table is ours. In relaxed speech our reduces to /ɑr/ and collides with are and with hour, which is why ✗ are house shows up in casual writing. English does not distinguish inclusive our (you and I) from exclusive our (my group, not you) — only context does.
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to, produced by, or associated with a group that includes the speaker.
examples: Our flight was delayed three hours. (singular countable)
Our neighbors repainted their porch. (plural countable)
Half our budget goes to rent. (predeterminer half; half of our budget is equally correct)
This one is our own fault.
We lost our luggage on the way back. (uncountable)
All our records are backed up offsite.
Is this our gate or the next one over? (question)
We haven't gotten our deposit back yet. (negative)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (their house), plural countable (their kids), uncountable (their time) — and gerunds (their leaving). The possessor may be plural, or a single person whose gender is unknown, unspecified, irrelevant, or nonbinary (singular they). Never another central determiner: ✗ the their house.
entries.ofRule: None of its own; of before their belongs to a preceding quantifier: none of their arguments, two of their kids. The double genitive uses theirs: a client of theirs.
entries.pattern: their [noun] · [predeterminer] their [noun] — all their friends, both their cars · their own [noun] · [quantifier] of their [noun]
entries.contrast: A four-way trap: their (determiner, noun follows), theirs (pronoun, nothing follows), there (a place, or the dummy subject in there is), and they're (= they are). ✗ their's is not a word. Against his or her: singular their is the ordinary spoken form and is now accepted by AP and Chicago; his or her is the formal written alternative and turns clumsy the moment it repeats.
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to, produced by, or associated with the possessor(s) already identified. 1. A plural possessor: the Wilsons sold their house. 2. Singular they — one person of unknown, unspecified, or nonbinary gender: Somebody left their umbrella. The noun stays singular if the referent has only one (Everyone brought their own lunch), and the verb still agrees with the subject, not with their. 3. An institution treated as a group of people: They raised their rates again. American editing normally prefers its for a named organization — the company raised its rates.
examples: Their flight lands before ours. (singular countable)
Both their kids play soccer. (predeterminer both; both of their kids is equally correct)
Somebody left their umbrella in the lobby. (singular they)
If a patient misses their appointment, the clinic charges a fee.
The Wilsons sold their house in March.
Everyone brought their own lunch. (everyone takes a singular verb — brought is neutral, but Everyone is bringing their own lunch, never ✗ Everyone are)
We never did get their luggage back. (uncountable, negative)
Did the Hills sell their boat? (question)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (your seat), plural countable (your kids), uncountable (your luggage) — and gerunds (your coming). One form covers a singular and a plural addressee. Never another central determiner: ✗ the your seat.
entries.ofRule: None of its own; of before your belongs to a preceding quantifier: some of your questions, each of your options. The double genitive uses yours: a friend of yours.
entries.pattern: your [noun] · [predeterminer] your [noun] — all your files, half your salary · your [ordinal] [cardinal] [noun] — your last two emails · your own [noun] · your [gerund] — your coming on short notice
entries.contrast: your + noun, yours alone, you're = you are. The test is expansion: ✗ Your welcome fails as your are welcome, so it must be You're welcome. In fast speech your and you're both reduce to /jɚ/, which is exactly why the pair is confused so often.
variants: regional plural forms — y'all's and emphatic all y'all's (Southern), you guys' (general informal), yinz's (Pittsburgh), youse's (New York, Philadelphia, Chicago), you-uns' / you'uns' (Appalachian and the Ohio Valley). All are informal speech, and edited writing uses your for both numbers; see y'all's for the pronunciations and the regional detail.
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to, produced by, or associated with the person or people addressed. 1. The ordinary possessive. 2. Generic or impersonal you, meaning "people in general": Your average commuter spends an hour in traffic. Informal; formal writing uses the average commuter or one's. 3. Before a gerund, naming the doer: I appreciate your coming.
examples: Is this your seat? (question, singular countable)
Your passport and your boarding pass, please.
I appreciate your coming on such short notice. (gerund)
All your files were backed up overnight. (predeterminer all + plural countable)
Do it your own way.
Your average commuter spends an hour a day in traffic. (generic your)
Don't forget your badge. (negative imperative)
We couldn't find your baggage on the carousel. (uncountable)

entries.ipa: /hɪz/, weak /ɪz/ — and the weak form is the whole point: unstressed, John his book and John's book are the same string of sounds
entries.position: central — the possessor noun and his together fill the one central slot
entries.register: obsolete Early Modern English; an American meets it only on Renaissance title pages, in the Book of Common Prayer, and in colonial deeds, wills, and inventories
entries.goesWith: the noun possessed may be singular countable (John his book), plural countable (the Duke his men), or uncountable (the Bishop his patience). The real restriction is on the possessor, which must be a full noun — normally a personal name or a title — sitting immediately in front of his: ✓ Thomas Hooker his farm, ✗ he his farm, ✗ somebody his farm. It cannot be stacked on a possessed noun that already has a determiner (✗ John his the book), and nothing may precede the phrase (✗ the John his book), because the whole thing is the central determiner.
entries.ofRule: No of-form of its own. The ordinary alternative in the same period was the plain of-genitive — the fall of Sejanus, the farm of Thomas Hooker. There is no double genitive built on it: ✗ a book of John his; Early Modern English wrote a book of John's.
entries.pattern: [possessor noun] his [noun] — John his book · [feminine possessor] her [noun] — Mistress Sands her jointure · [plural possessor] their [noun] — the Commons their petition · frozen survival — for Jesus Christ his sake
entries.contrast: Not the same thing as the possessive determiner his, which needs no possessor spelled out in front of it: his book names an owner already known, while John his book names him twice over. Against 's (singular genitive): the two were homophones — unstressed his is /ɪz/, and so is the -es of older Johnes book — which is why Early Modern writers, and the King James translators after them, sometimes wrote the pronoun out in full. The folk etymology that grew out of the resemblance is false: the 's ending descends from the Old English genitive -es and is centuries older than this construction, and a feminine possessor took her, which no contraction of his could ever produce. The mistaken belief did leave one permanent mark, though — it helped fix the apostrophe in 's, on the theory that a letter had been dropped.
variants: the pronoun matches the possessor, so the same construction also runs as her with a feminine possessor (Elizabeth her letters) and as their with a plural one (the Commons their petition). Grammar books call the whole set the his-genitive or the periphrastic genitive.
entries.meaning: The dead rival of the 's ending: a genitive built by naming the possessor and then adding a matching possessive pronoun after it. Recognize it; never write it.
examples: Sejanus his Fall is the title Ben Jonson put on his tragedy when it was printed in 1605 — the shape an American is likeliest to meet. (singular countable)
The Prayer Book collect ends …for Jesus Christ his sake. (the one frozen survival still read aloud)
A 1639 deed records Thomas Hooker his farm on the east bank of the river. (colonial land record — the other place it turns up)
The Duke his men were quartered in the town all winter. (plural countable)
Mistress Sands her jointure was entered in the parish book. (feminine possessor takes her, never ✗ his)
The Commons their petition was read aloud to the King. (plural possessor takes their)
Is that Cotton Mather his diary in the case, or a facsimile? (question)
The Bishop his patience was not inexhaustible. (uncountable, negative)
No American clerk would draft ✗ the plaintiff his signature today; the construction died out in the eighteenth century. (negative — modern legal drafting uses the plaintiff's signature)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (his or her locker), plural countable (his or her dependents), uncountable (his or her luggage). The restriction is on the possessor, not on the noun possessed: the possessor must be one person of unknown or unspecified gender (each employee … his or her contact information). A plural possessor takes their, never ✗ the employees … his or her lockers. Never another central determiner: ✗ the his or her locker.
entries.ofRule: None of its own; of before it belongs to a preceding quantifier (each of his or her dependents). The matching standalone pronoun is his or hers, awkward enough that writers rewrite the sentence instead.
entries.pattern: his or her [singular noun] · his or her own [noun] · variants his/her, her or his, his, her, or their
entries.contrast: The formal-register alternative to singular their. Their is shorter, accepted by AP and Chicago, and includes people who use they for themselves; his or her excludes them and becomes unreadable when repeated across a paragraph. In practice the best fix is usually neither one: make the noun plural — All employees must update their emergency contacts. Against generic his: his or her was the 1980s repair for generic his, and singular their has since largely replaced both. Agreement: the antecedent that licenses his or her is grammatically singular, so it takes a singular verb — ✓ Each employee is responsible for his or her own equipment, ✗ Each employee are; ✓ Every candidate submits his or her transcript, ✗ Every candidate submit. The same holds for either, neither, and anyone: ✓ Neither applicant has withdrawn his or her name. Choosing singular their instead does not change the verb — ✓ Each employee is responsible for their own equipment.
entries.meaning: Names a possessor who is one unidentified person, without committing to a gender.
examples: Each employee must update his or her emergency contact. (each + singular countable)
Every candidate submitted his or her transcript by the deadline. (every + singular countable)
Each participant is responsible for his or her travel expenses. (plural countable noun, singular verb is)
A juror may not discuss the case with his or her spouse. (negative)
Anyone who parked in Lot C should move his or her car.
No child may enter the pool without his or her parent.
Every applicant must show that his or her experience is relevant. (uncountable)
Has each of the finalists submitted his or her portfolio? (question; each of the requires of)

entries.ipa: /maɪn/ — no weak form. My reduces to /mə/ in ordinary speech, but this word survives only inside stressed, quoted phrases and never reduces
entries.register: archaic — biblical, liturgical, hymn, and poetic English. An American meets it in the King James Bible, in Shakespeare, in hymnals, and in the Battle Hymn of the Republic, and essentially nowhere else. Never in ordinary speech or modern prose.
entries.goesWith: any noun beginning with a vowel sound — singular countable (mine host, mine enemy), plural countable (mine eyes, mine ears), uncountable (mine iniquity) — plus the emphasizer own (mine own self). The vowel is the whole condition, so before a consonant sound the determiner is my: ✗ mine car, ✗ mine father, ✗ mine book. Seventeenth-century printing extends it before h- as well (mine heart, mine house), where the h was weak or silent. Never another central determiner: ✗ the mine eyes, ✗ a mine friend. Never with nothing after it — that is the pronoun mine.
entries.ofRule: None of its own. The of-phrase a friend of mine looks like this word and is not: there mine is the possessive pronoun filling the double genitive, and it is ordinary modern English. See of mine.
entries.pattern: mine [vowel-initial noun] — mine eyes, mine enemy · mine own [noun] — mine own self, mine own people · the alternation — my [consonant-initial noun] ~ mine [vowel-initial noun], as in my God but mine enemies · vocative — mine host
entries.contrast: Two different words are spelled mine, and only one of them is archaic. The determiner has a noun after it (mine eyes) and has been dead for four centuries; the possessive pronoun has nothing after it (that seat is mine, a friend of mine) and is perfectly ordinary today. That split is why mine looks alive while mine eyes looks like costume. Against my: one word, two shapes, chosen by the sound that begins the next word — the same machinery as a ~ an, and my hand / mine eyes is the pair to remember. Against thine: identical rule, one person over.
variants: my is the same determiner in its other shape, and the pair runs exactly parallel to thy ~ thine one person over.
Early Modern printing also spells it myne.

It has no modern or regional survival as a determiner: the -n forms still heard in Appalachian and Ozark speech (hisn, hern, ourn, yourn, theirn) were built by analogy with mine and thine, but they stand alone and are pronouns, not determiners — see Notes and tricky cases.
entries.meaning: The prevocalic shape of my, frozen inside quotation: it stands before a vowel sound the way an does. Recognize it; never write it.
examples: Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord. (the Battle Hymn of the Republic — plural countable, and the line most Americans know the form from)
Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace … for mine eyes have seen thy salvation. (Luke 2:29–30, King James Version)
Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God. (Psalm 59:1, KJV — both shapes in one line: mine before a vowel, my before a consonant)
Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee. (Psalm 119:11, KJV — the older extension of mine before h-)
Thou mine inheritance, now and always. (the hymn Be Thou My Vision — uncountable, and the title itself shows my before a consonant)
Mine host of the Garter kept the best cellar in Windsor. (Shakespeare's form of address to an innkeeper — singular countable)
Is that mine host at the door, or a stranger? (question, in deliberate period pastiche — the only way a modern writer produces the form on purpose)
✗ Mine car is in the shop is wrong twice over: the alternation needs a vowel sound, and the determiner died out in the seventeenth century. (negative — the error, not the word)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (one's passport), plural countable (one's options), uncountable (one's temper). The possessor is the generic pronoun one, meaning "a person, anyone," and standard usage keeps one … one's consistent through the sentence. Never another central determiner: ✗ the one's temper.
entries.ofRule: Only in the fixed phrase of one's own — a room of one's own, a place of one's own.
entries.pattern: One … one's [noun] · one's own [noun] · [noun] of one's own · [gerund phrase] — losing one's temper
entries.contrast: Three meanings, two spellings. One's with an apostrophe is the possessive (one's own business); ones without one is the plural of the noun or pronoun one (the red ones); and one's — the same spelling as the possessive — is also a contraction of one is or one has (one's never sure). Against your: American English almost always switches generic one to generic you — You should mind your own business is the everyday version, while One should mind one's own business reads as British or stiff. Older American usage shifted the possessive to his (One should mind his own business); that is now dated.
entries.meaning: Names a possessor who is anyone at all, in the impersonal generic construction.
examples: One should mind one's own business. (singular countable)
It is easy to lose one's temper in traffic. (uncountable)
One needs a room of one's own.
Losing one's passport abroad is a nightmare.
One rarely regrets holding one's tongue.
Keeping one's options open is generally good advice. (plural countable)
One cannot always trust one's first impression. (negative)
Where does one file one's appeal? (question)

entries.ipa: /ðaɪn/ — no weak form; the word only ever turns up stressed
entries.register: archaic — the King James Bible, the Book of Common Prayer, Shakespeare, hymns, and deliberate period writing. A few conservative Quaker meetings still keep the plain speech (thee, thy, thine) as a religious practice; outside that, an American reads this word and never says it.
entries.goesWith: any noun beginning with a vowel sound, with a single, familiar addressee — the thou of older English — so singular countable (thine enemy), plural countable (thine eyes, thine ears), uncountable (thine anger), plus the emphasizer own (thine own self). Before a consonant sound the determiner is thy: ✗ thine name, ✗ thine sword, ✗ thine father. Seventeenth-century printing extends it before h- as well (thine heart, thine house). A plural addressee never takes it — that is your. Never another central determiner: ✗ the thine eyes. Never with nothing after it — that is the pronoun thine.
entries.ofRule: None. There is no double genitive built on the determiner: Early Modern English wrote a friend of thine, where thine is the pronoun.
entries.pattern: thine [vowel-initial noun] — thine eyes · thine own [noun] — thine own self · the alternation — thy [consonant-initial noun] ~ thine [vowel-initial noun], as in thy whole body but thine eye · pronoun use, nothing following — the kingdom is thine
entries.contrast: Two words are spelled thine, and the test is the usual one: a noun after it makes it a determiner (thine eyes), nothing after it makes it a pronoun (the kingdom is thine, what's mine is thine). Against thy: one word, two shapes, chosen by the sound that begins the next word, exactly as a ~ an is. Against your: modern English lost the familiar singular altogether, so your now covers everything thy and thine used to. The standard beginner's mistake is sprinkling thine on any noun to sound old — ✗ thine sword, ✗ thine kingdom. The rule is mechanical, and it is about the next sound, not about solemnity.
variants: thy is the same determiner in its other shape; see thy for the pair treated together.
Early Modern printing also spells it thyne.
The first-person twin is mine, and the machinery is identical.
entries.meaning: The prevocalic shape of thy: the possessive of one familiar addressee, standing before a vowel sound the way an does. Recognize it; never write it outside quotation.
examples: To thine own self be true. (Polonius in Hamlet — the line most Americans can quote, with thine before the emphasizer own)
Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty. (Isaiah 33:17, King James Version — plural countable)
If thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. (Matthew 6:22, KJV — both shapes in one verse: thine before a vowel, thy before a consonant)
Trust in the Lord with all thine heart, and lean not unto thine own understanding. (Proverbs 3:5, KJV — the older extension before h-, then thine own)
We are consumed by thine anger, and by thy wrath are we troubled. (Psalm 90:7, KJV — uncountable)
Cast out first the beam out of thine own eye. (Luke 6:42, KJV — singular countable)
Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart? (2 Kings 10:15, KJV — question)
✗ Thine sword is the beginner's error every time: sword begins with a consonant sound, so the phrase is thy sword. (negative — the error, not the word)

entries.register: archaic — liturgical, biblical, poetic, or deliberately old-fashioned
entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (thy name), plural countable (thine eyes), uncountable (thy mercy) — with a singular and familiar addressee (the thou of older English). The form thy comes before a consonant sound and thine before a vowel sound. Never another central determiner: ✗ the thy hand.
entries.ofRule: None. The standalone pronoun is thine — the kingdom is thine.
entries.pattern: thy [consonant-initial noun] — thy name · thine [vowel-initial noun] — thine eyes · thine own [noun]
entries.contrast: The thy ~ thine alternation copies a ~ an exactly, and for the same reason: it smooths the join between words. Modern English collapsed the singular/plural and familiar/formal distinctions, so your now does every job that thy and your once split. You will meet thy only in the King James Bible, Shakespeare, hymns, and deliberate archaism — never write it in ordinary prose.
variants: thine /ðaɪn/ (THYNE) — not a separate word but the prevocalic shape of this same determiner, used before a vowel sound exactly as an is: thine eyes, thine enemy, thine own self, thine heart (older texts extend it before h- as well). It is also the standalone possessive pronoun — the kingdom is thine, what's mine is thine — so the test is the usual one: a noun after it makes it a determiner, nothing after it makes it a pronoun. An American meets thine in the King James Bible, in Shakespeare, and in hymns, and nowhere else; see thine for the full entry.
thy is to thou what your is to you
entries.meaning: Names a single, familiar addressee as the possessor; the ancestor of singular your.
examples: Hallowed be thy name. (singular countable)
Honor thy father and thy mother.
To thine own self be true. (thine before a vowel sound)
Thy rod and thy staff, they comfort me.
Open thine eyes and look around you. (plural countable)
O death, where is thy sting? (question)
Thy mercy endureth forever. (uncountable)
Take not thy hand from mine. (negative, in the archaic word order that goes with it)

entries.register: informal Southern and South Midland American speech; nonstandard in edited writing
entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (y'all's car), plural countable (y'all's kids), uncountable (y'all's help). The addressee is plural, or a singular addressee understood together with their household or group. Never another central determiner: ✗ the y'all's car.
entries.ofRule: None. The same form doubles as the standalone pronoun: that seat is y'all's.
entries.pattern: y'all's [noun] · all y'all's [noun] (emphatic, larger group)
entries.contrast: Standard English uses one your for both singular and plural addressees, and regional Englishes have repeatedly built a plural to fill the gap. These forms are unremarkable in speech within their regions and out of place in formal writing, where your covers both numbers. Note the two apostrophes in y'all's: one for the contracted you all, one for the possessive. Flagged clearly here because a learner needs to recognize it, not to write it.
variants: all y'all's /ˌɔl ˈjɔlz/ (awl YAWLZ) — the emphatic form, addressing every member of a larger group: All y'all's cars are getting towed.

parallel regional plural-you possessives, every one built the same way (a regional plural you plus 's): you'uns' / you-uns' /ˈjunz/ (YOONZ) — Appalachia and the Ohio Valley; yinz's /ˈjɪnzɪz/ (YINZ-iz) — Pittsburgh, where yinz is the worn-down local descendant of you'uns; youse's /ˈjuzɪz/ (YOO-ziz) — New York, Philadelphia, Chicago, and Irish-American speech; you guys' /ju ˈɡaɪz/ (yoo GYZE) — general informal American, the one form with no regional flag on it. Each takes any noun (you'uns' truck, yinz's kids, youse's help) and, like y'all's, doubles as the standalone pronoun (that one's yinz's). All are ordinary in speech where they are native and out of place on the page, where your covers both numbers.
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to the group being addressed. One entry covers the whole regional set: y'all's is the commonest of them, and all y'all's, you'uns', yinz's, youse's, and you guys' are the same determiner in the wording of a different region — they never contrast with one another, because no speaker has two of them.
examples: Is that y'all's dog out front? (question, singular countable)
We loved y'all's new place.
Y'all's flight got canceled too?
I'll need y'all's signatures on this form. (plural countable)
All y'all's excuses sound the same. (emphatic all y'all's — the whole larger group, Southern)
Thanks for y'all's help with the move. (uncountable)
We didn't get y'all's message until this morning. (negative)
Y'all's car is blocking the driveway.
Did yinz leave yinz's lights on again? (Pittsburgh speech, where yinz is the worn-down local descendant of you'uns)
You'uns' truck is settin' out there blockin' the gate. (Appalachian and Ohio Valley speech)
Youse's order is up at the counter. (New York, Philadelphia, Chicago, and Irish-American speech)

entries.position: postmodifier — not the central determiner slot
entries.goesWith: a head noun naming a part, property, or component of an inanimate antecedent — a house the roof of which leaks. That head noun may be singular countable (the roof of which), plural countable (the terms of which), or uncountable (the funding of which). Because of which is a prepositional phrase and not a determiner, the head noun keeps its own determiner: the roof of which, three floors of which.
entries.ofRule: Of is part of the item itself and is obligatory. Two legal orders: postposed (the roof of which) and fronted (of which the roof), the second more formal still.
entries.pattern: [antecedent], [determiner] [noun] of which [verb] … · [antecedent], of which [determiner] [noun] [verb] …
entries.contrast: The formal alternative to relative whose with a non-human antecedent. Whose is fully standard with things — a house whose roof leaks — and far more natural; of which belongs to legal, academic, and technical registers where some writers still avoid whose for inanimates. With a human antecedent only whose works: ✓ the man whose car was stolen, ✗ the man the car of which was stolen.
entries.meaning: Links a relative clause to its antecedent by naming something the antecedent has or contains.
examples: She cited a study the conclusions of which have since been retracted. (plural countable head — verb have)
It is an old contract, the terms of which nobody remembers.
The building, the top three floors of which are vacant, sold last month.
He owns a vineyard of which the yield has doubled in five years. (fronted order)
They passed a rule the effect of which was to end the program. (singular countable head — verb was)
This is the only clause the meaning of which is genuinely disputed.
It was a grant the funding of which has never been accounted for. (uncountable head, negative)
Is that the statute the wording of which is under review? (question)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (whose car), plural countable (whose keys), uncountable (whose money). The possessor may be a person, an animal, or a thing (a novel whose ending nobody likes). It fills the central determiner slot, so ✗ the whose car and ✗ a whose idea are impossible.
entries.ofRule: None as a determiner. The partitive question uses which: Which of these is yours? When whose takes no following noun it is a pronoun, not a determiner: Whose is this?
entries.pattern: Whose [noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? — Whose car is that? · [antecedent noun] whose [noun] [verb] … (relative) · I don't know whose [noun] it is. (embedded question) · Whose is this? (pronoun — no noun follows)
entries.contrast: whose versus who's. Whose asks or states possession; who's is the contraction of who is or who has. Expand it to test: Who's calling? = who is calling, but Whose call is it? has no expansion, so it takes whose. Against of which: both build an inanimate genitive relative, and whose is the ordinary choice (a car whose brakes failed), of which the formal one. Against which: which selects an item from a set (Which car?), whose asks who owns it (Whose car?).
entries.meaning: 1. Interrogative — asks which person or thing the following noun belongs to. 2. Relative — introduces a relative clause and ties its noun to the antecedent, for human and non-human antecedents alike.
examples: Whose jacket is on my chair? (question, singular countable)
I have no idea whose idea this was. (embedded question)
The engineer whose design won the contract is only 29. (relative, human antecedent)
She's the one whose flight got canceled.
It's an old house whose wiring needs replacing. (relative, non-human antecedent, uncountable)
Whose keys are these, and whose car is blocking the driveway? (plural countable, then singular)
Nobody remembers whose money paid for it. (negative, uncountable)
Whose is this? (pronoun — no noun follows, so not a determiner here)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (whosever car), plural countable (whosever keys), uncountable (whosever property) — inside a free relative clause meaning "the one whose." Unlike whose, it supplies its own antecedent, so no noun precedes it. Never another central determiner: ✗ the whosever car.
entries.ofRule: None.
entries.pattern: Whosever [noun] [verb] …, [main clause] · [main clause] whosever [noun] [verb] … · everyday spoken equivalent: whoever's [noun]
entries.contrast: In American speech people say whoever's: Whoever's car that is needs to move it. Whosever is the tidy written form and rare enough to sound stilted. Do not confuse it with relative whose, which requires an antecedent noun (the man whose car…); whosever contains its own (whosever car…). Agreement: the free relative names one person, so a main verb takes the singular even when the noun inside the clause is plural — ✓ Whosever keys these are needs to claim them, ✗ …need to claim them.
variants: the ordinary spoken form is whoever's
entries.meaning: Introduces a clause that identifies a possessor without naming one — "the person whose."
examples: Whosever car is blocking the driveway needs to move it.
Whosever name is on the lease is responsible for the damage.
She promised the prize to whosever entry arrived first.
Whosever idea this was, it worked.
The court will notify whosever property is affected.
Whosever turn it is, the trash goes out tonight.
Whosever keys these are needs to come get them. (plural countable noun, singular main verb)
We will not release the car to whosever insurance pays first. (uncountable, negative)

entries.ipa: /s/ after a voiceless sound (Pat's /pæts/), /z/ after a voiced sound (Dan's /dænz/), /ɪz/ after a sibilant (Chris's /ˈkrɪsɪz/)
entries.position: central — the whole genitive phrase fills the slot
entries.goesWith: attaches to the end of a complete noun phrase, not to the head noun. The noun it then determines may be singular countable (Dan's car), plural countable (Dan's kids), or uncountable (Dan's patience). It cannot combine with an article or demonstrative on the same noun: ✗ the Dan's car, ✗ this Dan's car.
entries.ofRule: The rival construction is the of-genitive — the girl's name / the name of the girl. See of for which one to choose.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase]'s [noun] · [noun phrase]'s own [noun] · [predeterminer] [noun phrase]'s [noun] — all Dan's friends · [noun phrase]'s [ordinal] [cardinal] [noun] — Dan's first two jobs
entries.contrast: Three identical-sounding endings. 's marks possession (Dan's car); plain s marks a plural (the Smiths are away); and 's also contracts is and has (Dan's here = Dan is here). Since the three are indistinguishable in speech, the apostrophe carries the whole load in writing — hence the greengrocer's ✗ apple's for sale. Against the plural genitive: the student's essays is one student, the students' essays is several. See s' (plural genitive).
entries.meaning: The productive genitive ending: it converts any noun phrase into a central determiner, and with a true possessor it makes the resulting phrase definite. (The measure genitive is the exception — two weeks' notice stays indefinite; see two weeks'.)
examples: That's my sister's car. (singular countable)
The dog's leash is by the door.
Chicago's winters are brutal. (plural countable)
Dan's patience finally ran out. (uncountable)
The senator's office issued a statement.
I borrowed my roommate's charger.
Isn't that Ana's apartment on the corner? (question)
We never got the landlord's approval. (negative)

entries.ipa: silent — the students' is pronounced exactly like the students /ðə ˈstudn̩ts/
entries.goesWith: a regular plural noun already ending in -s; the apostrophe goes after that s and nothing further is added. The noun it determines may be singular countable, plural countable, or uncountable: the teachers' lounge, the teachers' contracts, the teachers' patience. Irregular plurals that do not end in -s take a full 's instead — see the children's.
entries.ofRule: the of-genitive is the usual alternative for long or inanimate plural possessors: the conclusions of the reports.
entries.pattern: [regular plural noun]' [noun] — the teachers' lounge, the Johnsons' driveway · measure phrases: two weeks' notice, ten years' experience
entries.contrast: the student's essays = one student, several essays. The students' essays = several students. ✗ The students essays = a missing apostrophe. Placement is the only signal and it is completely inaudible, which is why plural possessives get checked so hard in editing. Family names pluralize first, then take the apostrophe: the Johnsons → the Johnsons' house; never ✗ the Johnson's house for a family. Against the descriptive plural, which takes no apostrophe at all: a farmers market, a teachers college, a veterans hospital, Publishers Weekly — here the plural noun names the kind of thing rather than an owner, and American style guides drop the apostrophe. Ask whether the sense is ownership (the teachers' contracts) or description (a teachers college).
entries.meaning: The plural counterpart of 's: same job, same silence, different apostrophe placement.
examples: The teachers' lounge is on the second floor. (singular countable head — verb is, agreeing with lounge, not with teachers)
We repaved the Johnsons' driveway.
All the players' contracts expire in June. (plural countable head — verb expire)
The workers' patience ran out in the third week. (uncountable)
That's the girls' locker room.
Both parties' lawyers agreed to a delay. (predeterminer both + plural)
Isn't that the neighbors' dog again? (question)
The owners' association has not met since March. (negative)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (Anna and Ben's cabin), plural countable (Anna and Ben's kids), uncountable (Anna and Ben's furniture). One 's, on the last name only, means joint possession (Anna and Ben's house — one house). An 's on each name means separate possession, and the following noun is then usually plural (Anna's and Ben's houses — two houses).
entries.ofRule: The of-genitive sidesteps the ambiguity but sounds stiff with people: the cabin of Anna and Ben.
entries.pattern: [Name] and [Name]'s [noun] — joint · [Name]'s and [Name]'s [plural noun] — separate · [Name]'s and my [noun] — with a first-person partner
entries.contrast: The single-'s pattern is another consequence of the ending attaching to the phrase: Anna and Ben is one noun phrase, so it takes one ending. When a pronoun joins the coordination the pattern breaks, because pronouns have their own possessive forms: ✓ Ben's and my apartment, ✗ Ben and my apartment, ✗ me and Ben's apartment (common in speech, nonstandard in writing).
entries.meaning: Marks two or more possessors, with the apostrophe placement showing whether they own the thing together or separately.
examples: We spent the weekend at Anna and Ben's cabin. (joint, singular countable)
Anna and Ben's wedding is in October.
Anna's and Ben's families have never met. (separate, plural countable)
Ben's and my apartment is on the third floor.
The judge compared the plaintiff's and the defendant's accounts.
Mom and Dad's anniversary is Sunday.
All of Anna and Ben's furniture came from the same store. (uncountable)
Isn't that Anna and Ben's dog? (question)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (Chris's desk), plural countable (Chris's parents), uncountable (Chris's luggage). The possessor is a singular name or noun that already ends in -s or another sibilant — Chris, the boss, the witness, Texas, Dickens.
entries.ofRule: The of-genitive is an escape hatch when the pile-up is ugly: the policies of Congress rather than Congress's policies. Both are correct.
entries.pattern: [singular name or noun ending in a sibilant]'s [noun] — Chris's desk, the boss's office, Texas's economy
entries.contrast: This is a spelling choice, not a grammar one — Chris's and Chris' are the same word and most Americans pronounce both /ˈkrɪsɪz/. Pick one style guide and stay consistent. Keep it separate from the plural the Chrises and from the plural possessive the Joneses' (family of Joneses → the Joneses' house).
variants: the two American style guides split, and they split differently for names than for common nouns. AP uses the bare apostrophe for a singular proper name ending in s (Chris', Dickens', Texas') but a full 's for a singular common noun (the boss's office, the witness's testimony). Chicago, and book publishing generally, adds 's to both (Chris's, the boss's). Classical and biblical names traditionally take the bare apostrophe — Jesus', Moses', Achilles' — a convention AP keeps and Chicago has since folded back into its general 's rule. The fixed phrases for goodness' sake and for conscience' sake keep the bare apostrophe everywhere.
entries.meaning: The singular genitive of a possessor that already ends in a hissing sound, where the extra syllable is heard but the extra s is optional in print.
examples: Chris's desk is the one by the window. (singular countable)
The boss's office is at the end of the hall.
Chris's parents are flying in on Thursday. (plural countable)
Texas's economy grew faster than the national average. (uncountable)
The witness's testimony contradicted the report.
She quoted Dickens's description of the fog.
Isn't that James's car out front? (question)
The hostess's name was not on the list. (negative)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (each other's car), plural countable (each other's kids), uncountable (each other's mail). The possessors are two or more people or things in a crosswise relation, so the subject of the clause is always plural; the possessive phrase itself stays singular in shape. Never another central determiner: ✗ the each other's sentences.
entries.ofRule: No of-form of its own; of before it belongs to a preceding quantifier (several of each other's clients). Keep the genitive apart from the plain of-phrase, which means something different: photos of each other are photos they appear in, while each other's photos are the photos they own.
entries.pattern: [plural subject] [plural verb] each other's [noun] · [plural subject] [plural verb] one another's [noun] · in / on / at each other's [noun] — they slept at each other's houses
entries.contrast: The apostrophe never moves, however many possessors there are: ✓ each other's names, ✗ each others' names, ✗ each others names. Each other is a fixed singular-shaped phrase, so the ending lands where it would on any singular. Against their own: They graded their own papers means each graded the paper he or she wrote; They graded each other's papers means the grading went crosswise. Against both: both their cars is two cars owned one apiece, while each other's cars is the swap. Agreement: the subject is plural, so the verb is plural — ✓ The twins wear each other's clothes, ✗ The twins wears. The noun after each other's can be singular or plural on its own terms: they finished each other's sentences, they parked in each other's spot.
variants: one another's — the formal-register twin. The old schoolroom rule reserved each other for two and one another for three or more, but American usage treats them as interchangeable and no editor enforces the split.
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to the members of a group taken crosswise — each of them to the other.
examples: They finished each other's sentences all evening. (plural countable)
The two teams studied each other's playbooks.
We borrowed each other's notes before the exam.
The roommates keep opening each other's mail. (uncountable)
The partners countersigned one another's forms. (formal variant)
The two candidates attacked each other's voting record. (singular countable)
Are those two still parking in each other's spots? (question)
The sisters never wear each other's clothes. (negative)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (John's car), plural countable (John's parents), uncountable (John's luggage). The possessor is a personal name, which is the most natural possessor of all for the s-genitive.
entries.ofRule: The of-genitive is grammatical but marked with people — the car of John sounds foreign. Use the s-genitive with human possessors. The one everyday of pattern is the double genitive: a book of John's.
entries.pattern: [proper name]'s [noun] · [proper name]'s own [noun] · [predeterminer] [proper name]'s [noun] — all John's friends · [proper name]'s [ordinal] [cardinal] [noun] — John's first two novels
entries.contrast: A genitive proper name is the determiner, so it blocks every other one: ✓ John's book, ✗ the John's book, ✗ a John's book. To keep the noun indefinite, use the double genitive — a book of John's. Plural family names take the plural genitive (the Johnsons'), and a name ending in s becomes Chris's or Chris'.
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to a named person; also the standard way to attach an author, inventor, or origin to a noun.
examples: John's car is in the shop. (singular countable)
Have you met John's parents? (question, plural countable)
Sarah's proposal impressed the whole committee.
The airline lost Miguel's luggage. (uncountable)
All John's friends showed up. (predeterminer all; all of John's friends is equally correct)
Lincoln's second inaugural address is carved on the wall.
Sarah's replacement has not been named. (negative)
We're borrowing Miguel's truck this weekend.

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (somebody else's problem), plural countable (somebody else's kids), uncountable (somebody else's money). The ending lands on else, the last word of the phrase, never on the pronoun: ✗ somebody's else problem.
entries.ofRule: No plain of-form; the indefinite version is the double genitive — a car of somebody else's.
entries.pattern: [indefinite pronoun] else's [noun] — somebody else's, someone else's, anybody else's, everyone else's, nobody else's, who else's · bare indefinite genitive, no else — anybody's guess, nobody's business, everyone's problem
entries.contrast: The clearest small proof that 's attaches to a phrase, not a word: else is not the possessor, but it ends the phrase, so it carries the ending — the same mechanism as the King of Spain's. Note also who else's (Who else's number do you have?) against the impossible ✗ whose else. Against each other's: somebody else's points outside the group, each other's points crosswise inside it. Agreement: the indefinite pronoun is singular, but when the genitive phrase heads the subject the verb follows the head noun, not the pronoun — Somebody else's kids were in the pool (plural kids), Somebody else's kid was in the pool (singular kid).
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to an unnamed person other than the one already mentioned.
examples: That's somebody else's problem now. (singular countable)
Don't take anybody else's word for it. (negative imperative)
Everyone else's flights were on time. (plural countable)
It was nobody else's fault but mine.
She was wearing someone else's coat.
Who else's signature do we need on this? (question)
Nobody wants to clean up somebody else's mess. (uncountable)
Anybody's guess is as good as mine. (bare indefinite genitive, no else)

entries.position: fills the entire noun phrase — the head noun is deleted
entries.goesWith: no following noun at all. The noun the genitive would have determined — shop, house, office, church, place — is understood and left out: at the butcher's = at the butcher's shop; at Ana's = at Ana's place.
entries.ofRule: None.
entries.pattern: [preposition] the [tradesperson]'s — at the butcher's, to the dentist's · [preposition] [personal name]'s — at Ana's, at my grandmother's · [business or church name]'s — Macy's, St. Paul's
entries.contrast: An ordinary genitive is a determiner because a noun follows it; the elliptical genitive is a complete noun phrase with the noun missing, so it determines nothing. American English keeps the head noun more often than British English — at the doctor's office, the dry cleaner's — and many American business names froze in this shape with no shop word ever following: Macy's, Wendy's, Lowe's, Trader Joe's.
entries.meaning: Names a place by naming the person or business that occupies it, with the word for the place left unsaid.
examples: She's at the dentist's until noon.
I picked up the shirts from the dry cleaner's.
We had dinner at Ana's last night.
They got married at St. Paul's.
Meet me outside Macy's on 34th Street.
He spent the afternoon at his grandmother's.
Aren't you going to the butcher's first? (question)
We didn't stop at the pharmacist's on the way home. (negative)

entries.goesWith: any noun. The possessor is a plural noun that does not end in -s — children, men, women, people, mice, geese, feet, alumni. The determined noun may be singular countable (the children's table), plural countable (the children's coats), or uncountable (the children's luggage).
entries.ofRule: The of-genitive is available and often better with long phrases: the rights of the children who were separated at the border.
entries.pattern: the [irregular plural]'s [noun] — the children's books, the men's room, the women's team, the people's choice
entries.contrast: Regular plurals put the apostrophe after the s and add no sound (the students'); irregular plurals take a full 's and add a /z/ or a whole syllable (the children's). ✗ the childrens' and ✗ the childrens are both wrong, because children is already plural — same for ✗ the mens' room and ✗ the peoples' choice.
entries.meaning: The genitive of a plural that forms itself without -s, which therefore takes the ordinary singular-shaped ending.
examples: The children's coats are in the hall closet. (plural countable head — verb are)
The men's room is around the corner. (singular countable head — verb is)
She coaches the women's soccer team.
It won the people's choice award three years running.
The children's luggage never made it onto the plane. (uncountable, negative)
The mice's nest was behind the water heater.
Where is the children's section in this library? (question)
The alumni's donations covered the whole renovation.

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (the company's headquarters), plural countable (the company's employees), uncountable (the company's revenue). The possessor is an organization, a place, a publication, a vehicle, or another inanimate noun rather than a person.
entries.ofRule: The of-genitive is the direct competitor and is often better when the possessor is long or heavily modified: ✓ the company's policy, ✓ the policy of the company that acquired us last spring.
entries.pattern: the [organization]'s [noun] · [place name]'s [noun] — Chicago's winters · the [publication]'s [noun] — the Times's editorial
entries.contrast: The old schoolroom rule that only living things take the s-genitive is out of date. Organizations, cities, countries, publications, vehicles, and time expressions all take it freely in American English: the city's budget, the report's conclusion, the car's warranty. What still resists it are ordinary concrete objects and their physical parts — ✓ the leg of the table over awkward the table's leg, ✓ the roof of the house over the house's roof. See of for the full decision.
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to, produced by, or characteristic of an institution or other non-human entity.
examples: The company's stock dropped nine percent overnight. (uncountable)
The city's budget passed on a 7–4 vote. (singular countable)
The report's conclusion contradicts its own data.
The company's employees were not told until Friday. (plural countable, negative)
The university's enrollment is up for the third year.
The car's warranty expires in March.
Has the Times's editorial board endorsed anyone yet? (question)
The city's revenue has not recovered. (uncountable, negative)

entries.register: neutral in speech; avoided in edited writing when long
entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (the King of Spain's daughter), plural countable (the King of Spain's daughters), uncountable (the King of Spain's luggage). The ending attaches to the last word of the whole possessor phrase, even when that word is not the possessor: in the King of Spain's daughter, the daughter belongs to the King, not to Spain.
entries.ofRule: The of-genitive is usually the cleaner choice when the possessor phrase is long: the daughter of the King of Spain.
entries.pattern: [determiner] [noun] [postmodifier]'s [noun] — the King of Spain's daughter, the woman next door's cat, the guy I met yesterday's number
entries.contrast: Proof that 's is a phrase-level clitic, not a noun suffix: it lands on the end of the phrase, never on the head noun. ✗ the King's of Spain daughter is the classic error. Long group genitives are ordinary in speech and clumsy on the page, where the of-genitive is preferred: the number of the guy I met yesterday.
entries.meaning: Turns an entire modified noun phrase — article, head, and everything that follows it — into a single determiner.
examples: The King of Spain's daughter studied in the United States. (singular countable)
The woman next door's cat keeps getting into our garage.
The guy I met yesterday's number is in my phone somewhere.
The Secretary of State's plane landed in Rome this morning.
The head of marketing's proposals were all rejected. (plural countable)
Somebody I used to work with's brother owns the place. (natural in speech; rewrite it in edited prose)
The man in 4B's mail keeps coming to us. (uncountable)
Is that the woman next door's car in our spot? (question)

entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (today's paper), plural countable (today's numbers), uncountable (today's mail). The possessor is a time word: today, yesterday, tomorrow, tonight, this morning, last year, next week.
entries.ofRule: The of-genitive exists but is stiffer and rarer: the newspaper of today.
entries.pattern: today's [noun] · yesterday's / tomorrow's / tonight's [noun] · last year's / next week's [noun] · this morning's [noun]
entries.contrast: Time expressions take the s-genitive freely although they are not animate — one of the oldest exceptions to the animacy preference. Distinguish the genitive today's meeting (the meeting held today) from the measure genitive a day's work (work amounting to a day — see two weeks'). Note too that today, yesterday, and tomorrow cannot modify a noun bare — ✓ today's meeting, ✗ today meeting — even though day and month names can: ✓ the Monday meeting, ✓ a March deadline.
entries.meaning: Marks the following noun as belonging to, occurring on, or dated to a particular time.
examples: Did you read today's paper? (question, singular countable)
Yesterday's storm knocked out power on the whole block.
Tomorrow's numbers will not be final until noon. (plural countable, negative)
Last year's model is on clearance.
Tonight's game starts at seven.
This morning's email explains the change.
Today's mail is still on the porch. (uncountable)
Next week's schedule has not gone out yet. (negative)

entries.ipa: /tu ˈwiks/ — the apostrophe adds no sound
entries.goesWith: a noun naming an amount, period, or entitlement. That noun is normally uncountable (two weeks' notice, ten years' experience, three months' revenue, a dollar's worth, a day's work, two weeks' pay) or singular countable (an hour's drive, a moment's hesitation, a week's delay). Plural countable heads are rare and get rephrased: ✓ two weeks' worth of meals rather than the odd two weeks' meals. The possessor is a quantity of time, money, or distance rather than an owner.
entries.ofRule: Not used with of between the measure and its noun. The competing structure is a hyphenated attributive with no apostrophe and a singular unit: a two-week notice, a ten-year contract. Of does appear after the head noun in the partitive frame two weeks' worth of [noun].
entries.pattern: [number] [plural unit]' [noun] — two weeks' notice, ten years' experience · a / an [singular unit]'s [noun] — a day's work, an hour's drive, a dollar's worth
entries.contrast: The apostrophe is compulsory here and is dropped constantly: ✗ two weeks notice (the movie title notwithstanding). The apostrophe-free alternative uses a singular unit with a hyphen — a two-week vacation, a ten-dollar bill. So two weeks' pay and a two-week delay are both right, while ✗ a two-weeks delay and ✗ two week's pay are both wrong. Note also what this genitive does not do: unlike an ordinary possessive, it leaves the phrase indefinite. John's notice is definite, but two weeks' notice is not — which is why a day's work can still carry its own a (the a belongs to day, not to work). Agreement: the verb follows the head noun, not the number in the measure — ✓ Two weeks' notice is required, ✗ two weeks' notice are required; ✓ Ten years' experience is preferred.
entries.meaning: Expresses an amount as if it were a possessor: the notice that two weeks amounts to, the drive that an hour amounts to.
examples: She gave two weeks' notice on Friday. (uncountable)
Ten years' experience is preferred for this role. (singular verb is)
It's an hour's drive from the airport. (singular countable)
That's a full day's work right there.
I bought five dollars' worth of quarters for the laundry.
The strike cost them three months' revenue.
Isn't two weeks' notice the standard here? (question)
He didn't give them a moment's warning. (negative)

entries.type: genitive (of-genitive) — a preposition, not a determiner
entries.position: postmodifier; the head noun keeps its own determiner
entries.goesWith: links a head noun to a following noun phrase that owns, contains, produces, or defines it — the roof of the house. Each half keeps its own determiner, one on the head noun and another on the noun after of, which is exactly what the s-genitive cannot do. Any noun type can head the phrase: singular countable (the size of the room), plural countable (the members of the board), uncountable (the smell of the paint).
entries.ofRule: Of is the item itself. It requires a full noun phrase or a possessive pronoun after it, never a bare possessive determiner: ✓ of the house, ✓ of mine, ✗ of my. The partitive frame runs on its own schedule: all (of) the students leaves of optional, each of the students and most of the students require it, all of them requires it before a pronoun, and every never takes it at all — ✗ every of the students, ✓ every one of the students.
entries.pattern: [determiner] [head noun] of [noun phrase] — the title of the book · [determiner] [head noun] of [possessive pronoun] — a friend of mine (see of mine) · [quantifier] of [determiner + noun] — most of the students
entries.contrast: The choice between the girl's name and the name of the girl runs on three factors. Animacy — people and animals prefer 's (the girl's name), plain objects prefer of (the leg of the table). Weight — long or heavily modified possessors go after of (the proposal of the committee that met last Thursday). Focus — whatever lands last carries the emphasis. Institutions, places, publications, vehicles, and time words break the animacy preference and take 's freely; see the company's and today's.
entries.meaning: Builds a possessive relationship after the noun instead of before it, and takes over wherever the s-genitive is awkward.
examples: The roof of the house needs replacing. (singular countable head)
What's the title of the book you mentioned? (question)
The conclusion of the report that the auditors filed last spring was ignored.
The members of the board have not been notified. (plural countable head, negative)
He's a friend of my brother's. (double genitive)
The population of Chicago has been flat for a decade.
I can't stand the smell of the paint. (uncountable head)
Each of the applicants was interviewed twice. (each of the — of is obligatory, verb singular)

entries.position: postmodifier — it frees the central slot for a different determiner
entries.goesWith: a head noun already determined by a/an, a number, a demonstrative, or a quantifier — a friend of mine, two cousins of hers, that car of yours, several clients of ours. That head noun is normally countable — singular with a/an or a demonstrative (a friend of mine, this book of theirs), plural with a number or quantifier (two cousins of hers, several clients of ours). With an uncountable noun the construction is limited to demonstrative and evaluative uses: ✓ that attitude of yours, ✓ this nonsense of theirs, but ✗ a money of mine. The complement of of must be a possessive pronoun (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs) or a genitive noun phrase (of my father's, of John's) — never a possessive determiner: ✗ a friend of my.
entries.ofRule: Of is obligatory; the construction is nothing but of plus a possessive.
entries.pattern: [a/an / number / demonstrative / quantifier] [noun] of [mine / yours / his / hers / ours / theirs] · [same] [noun] of [name]'s — a friend of John's
entries.contrast: This construction exists because the central determiner slot holds exactly one item. You cannot say ✗ a my friend or ✗ that your car, so English pushes the possessive to the end. Note the meaning split against a plain of-phrase: a picture of my father has him in it, while a picture of my father's means he owns it. With a demonstrative the construction usually carries an attitude — that car of yours is rarely neutral.
entries.meaning: Combines possession with an indefinite, demonstrative, or quantified determiner, which the one-determiner rule otherwise forbids.
examples: She's an old friend of mine from college. (a/an + singular countable)
That car of yours is going to break down on the highway. (demonstrative)
Two cousins of his flew in for the funeral. (number + plural countable)
Several clients of ours asked the same question. (quantifier + plural countable)
He borrowed a jacket of my brother's and never returned it. (genitive noun phrase after of)
Is this book of theirs worth reading? (question)
That attitude of yours is not helping. (uncountable, evaluative, negative)
I have not met a single neighbor of theirs. (negative)

entries.position: postdeterminer, between the central determiner and the noun
entries.goesWith: any noun — singular countable (my own room), plural countable (her own reasons), uncountable (his own money) — but only when a possessive determiner or a genitive phrase comes first: ✓ my own room, ✓ John's own words, ✗ the own room, ✗ an own car. It may also precede a numeral: my own two hands.
entries.ofRule: Yes, in the fixed frame [noun] of [possessive pronoun] own — a place of her own, a room of one's own, ideas of his own.
entries.pattern: [possessive] own [noun] · [possessive] own [number] [noun] — my own two hands · on [possessive] own — she did it on her own · [determiner] [noun] of [possessive pronoun] own — a place of his own
entries.contrast: Own is an intensifier, not a determiner: it cannot open a noun phrase and it never replaces the possessive. Keep it apart from the verb own (she owns three rentals) and from the frozen soccer term an own goal, which is the one place English tolerates own with no possessive in front of it. Against each other's: their own rooms gives each person the room he or she owns, each other's rooms swaps them.
entries.meaning: Reinforces a possessive — "belonging to that person and to nobody else" — and blocks any reading in which the noun is shared.
examples: She paid for the trip with her own money. (uncountable)
Every state sets its own speed limits. (plural countable)
I built the shelves with my own two hands. (before a numeral)
He'd like a place of his own someday. (singular countable, of-frame)
They finished the whole project on their own.
Those were the mayor's own words, not mine. (after a genitive phrase)
Doesn't she have an office of her own yet? (question)
He never had a room of his own growing up. (negative)

entries.type: contraction of it is / it has
entries.position: none — it is a subject plus a verb, not part of a noun phrase
entries.register: neutral in speech and ordinary writing; spelled out in the most formal prose
entries.goesWith: nothing. It cannot precede a noun the way a determiner does. In It's a problem, the determiner is a, not it's.
entries.ofRule: Not applicable.
entries.pattern: It's [adjective] — It's cold. · It's [noun phrase] — It's a shame. · It's [verb]-ing — It's raining. · It's been [noun phrase] — It's been a week.
entries.contrast: ✗ The dog hurt it's paw → ✓ its paw. Expand it: the dog hurt it is paw is nonsense, so the possessive its is required. In the other direction, ✗ Its raining → ✓ It's raining. And ✗ its' is not a word in any sense at all — there is no situation in English that calls for it.
entries.meaning: The contraction of it is or it has; a determiner-shaped trap with no determiner function whatsoever.
examples: It's going to rain all weekend.
It's been three years since we moved.
I think it's your turn.
It's not the money, it's the principle.
It's a shame nobody told us sooner.
If it's broken, its warranty should cover the repair.

entries.register: neutral in speech and ordinary writing
entries.goesWith: nothing. No noun can follow it the way one follows their.
entries.ofRule: Not applicable.
entries.pattern: They're [adjective] · They're [verb]-ing · They're [noun phrase] · They're not / They aren't …
entries.contrast: Three homophones, one sound. Their is the possessive determiner (their house); there is a place or the dummy subject (over there, there is a problem); they're is they are. Expand to test: They're late = they are late, while ✗ Their late fails. Watch for a fourth error alongside these: ✗ their's is not a word — the pronoun is theirs.
entries.meaning: The contraction of they are; identical in sound to the possessive their and to the locative there.
examples: They're landing in about twenty minutes.
They're the only ones who showed up.
I don't know whether they're coming.
They're not going to like this.
They're fixing their roof over there this week.
If they're late again, we'll start without them.

entries.type: contraction of who is / who has
entries.goesWith: nothing. Compare Whose keys are these? (determiner plus noun) with Who's driving? (subject plus verb).
entries.ofRule: Not applicable.
entries.pattern: Who's [verb]-ing? · Who's [noun phrase]? · Who's been [verb]-ing? · [antecedent] who's … (relative who plus is)
entries.contrast: Expand to who is or who has. Who's coming? = who is coming; Whose car is that? has no expansion, so it takes the possessive whose. In speech the two are identical — /huz/ both times — which is why this error survives every spell-check.
entries.meaning: The contraction of who is or who has; the twin of the interrogative and relative determiner whose.
examples: Who's driving tonight?
Who's been using my desk?
Do you know who's in charge here?
She's the one who's always early.
Who's going to tell him whose idea it was?
Who's got the tickets?

entries.goesWith: nothing. It cannot precede a noun; You're the third caller has the as its determiner.
entries.ofRule: Not applicable.
entries.pattern: You're [adjective] · You're [verb]-ing · You're [noun phrase] · You're not / You aren't …
entries.contrast: ✗ Your welcome → ✓ You're welcome; ✗ You're keys are on the table → ✓ Your keys. Expand to you are. In fast speech both words reduce to /jɚ/, so the ear gives no help at all — this pair and its/it's are the two most frequently corrected apostrophe errors in English.
entries.meaning: The contraction of you are; identical in sound to the possessive determiner your.
examples: You're welcome.
You're going to love this place.
I think you're right about the schedule.
You're the third person to ask me that today.
If you're late, your seat goes to someone else.
You're not the one who has to explain it.
